draft.title: Qing China and the West
card: In the 1700s China was ruled by the Qing dynasty. It was large, rich and powerful, and it made goods that people overseas wanted, such as tea, silk and porcelain.
European merchants wanted to buy these goods. The Qing government did not want its trade controlled by foreigners, so it set the terms.
From 1757, European traders were limited to one port, Canton (now Guangzhou). They could trade only at certain times and with merchants approved by the Chinese government.
The Qing court saw little it needed from the West. Europeans had few goods China wanted, so they paid mostly in silver.
draft.remember: Qing China set the rules of trade because it was strong and wanted little from Europe.

a.q: Why did Qing China limit European traders to the port of Canton?
opts: It wanted to control trade on its own terms
It was too weak to defend its other ports
It had no goods that Europeans wanted to buy
It was at war with the European countries
a.why: China was strong and wealthy, so it could set the terms of trade and keep foreign merchants in one place. The idea that China was weak is tempting but wrong: in the 1700s it was powerful, and Europeans wanted its tea and silk.
a.clue: Think about who held the power in the 1700s.

b.q: In 1793 a British envoy asked the Qing emperor for wider trade. The emperor replied that China had all it needed and had no use for British goods. What does this show?
opts: The Qing saw little need to trade with the West
The Qing feared Britain's army and navy
The Qing needed British goods to stay rich
The Qing wanted trade open at every port
b.why: The emperor's reply shows a state that felt self-sufficient and saw little it needed from Europe. Fear of Britain is tempting, but the card shows China was strong and in control of trade at this time.
b.clue: Look at what the emperor says China already has.

a.best: It wanted to control trade on its own terms

b.best: The Qing saw little need to trade with the West
